title: Rate slice allocator and API key zoning demo - Vanguard AI
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Vanguard AI through org/project key zoning, the rate-slice allocator in the Console, and API-level backpressure patterns. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, VPC/KMS needs, and next steps for a pilot and security docs. Customer expressed interest in adaptive quotas but asked for more detail on multi-tenant fairness under bursty workloads.
next_steps: Alex to send tailored pricing for a 3-month pilot (includes Dedicated burst bandwidth)
Maya to share security pack (SOC2 summary, KMS integration guide, audit log export) by 2026-04-20
Schedule POC kickoff with infra team week of 2026-04-27
Tom and Maya to align on benchmark suite and token budget
action_items: Alex: Prepare pilot pricing and org/project key setup doc (due 2026-04-20)
Maya: Send security and network integration docs (due 2026-04-20)
Liam: Share traffic patterns and peak QPS examples (due 2026-04-22)

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-15 09:23 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Kim, Maya Patel, Jordan Lee - Redwood; Priya Rao (CTO), Liam O'Neal (Platform), Sara Gomez (SecOps), Tom Wu (ML) - Vanguard AI

[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Maya and Jordan from the product team are with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya Rao: Good morning, thanks for setting this up. We're excited to see how you handle multi-tenant quotas — our infra team has been wrestling with bursty traffic across projects.
[00:12] Maya Patel: Great, we'll walk through the Console first, show the rate-slice allocator and how org/project keys map to fairshare policies, and then demo API behaviors under simulated bursts.
[00:20] Liam O'Neal: Quick ask — we need to understand hosted vs dedicated latency/cost tradeoffs and how that impacts throttling. Also network egress for private VPC is key for us.
[00:28] Alex Kim: Perfect, we'll cover that. Real quick agenda: 1) Key zoning and org/project hierarchy, 2) Quota slices and adaptive allocator, 3) Demo traffic shaping and fallback to cheaper model variants, 4) Security & infra Qs.
[00:37] Jordan Lee: I'll start in the Console — here's the org dashboard, you can see projects pinned to specific pools and per-project token caps. Note: the UI shows both concurrency and token windows.
[00:50] [screen share noise] Jordan Lee: So this is a configured policy called "rate-slice-allocator-v2", it allocates capacity proportionally to project weights and will reserve a burst bucket for emergencies. The allocator checks per-token spend and active windows, then rebalances.
[01:12] Tom Wu: Does the allocation strategy preserve latency SLOs for high priority projects during spikes? Our recommendations team will need sub-200ms tail latency for inline recommender calls.
[01:20] Maya Patel: Yes you can set priority lanes; critical projects get reserved concurrency and soft limits for lower tiers. Under heavy load the allocator will degrade non-critical projects first and also can reroute to a cheaper quantized variant. Small caveat: if you use Dedicated with pinned GPUs you get better tail latency guarantees. Hosted can be cheaper but burst behavior may have slightly higher p99 under extreme tails.
[01:44] Sara Gomez: For security, what happens to logs and traces? We need audit logs for all token usage and user-level tracing — and KMS integration for key material.
[01:52] Maya Patel: We provide audit log export to your SIEM, S3 sinks, and KMS/HSM integration for private deployments. Note: some of our doc text calls it "key-store" which is slightly different in other vendors. We'll share the security pack.
[02:08] Priya Rao: Can you show the policy config for org vs project keys? We have product teams that want to delegate billing but keep network isolation.
[02:14] Jordan Lee: Sure — here is an example YAML policy. You can attach a policy to an org or override at a project level. The common pattern is org-level default quotas, project-level weights, and sticky routing so sessions map to the same project pool for KV cache locality.
[02:33] [transcription glitch] Jordan Lee: ...and the kay-vee cache, the KV cache, sorry — keeping latency down for chat contexts.
[02:40] Liam O'Neal: Sticky routing is important — our models do a lot of long-context calls and cold KV misses kill us.
[02:46] Maya Patel: Exactly. Also the Console has an Optimize recommendation engine that suggests quantization levels per model based on your token distribution to hit cost targets without dropping quality. We had a case recently where switching to 4-bit Q model saved 38% cost with negligible quality delta for embedding-heavy workloads.
[03:05] Tom Wu: How do you measure "negligible"? We need to run evaluation sets and see prompts before we commit.
[03:10] Jordan Lee: We plug into your eval harness — Redwood Optimize will run A/Bs and produce a delta report tied to your prompt set. We'll also surface regressions on the Console.
[03:20] Priya Rao: On the topic of governance, is SSO/SAML supported and can you do role-based RBAC so our SREs can only change routing, not billing?
[03:27] Alex Kim: Yes, SSO/SAML, SAML provisioning, SCIM for user sync, and RBAC with fine-grained permissions are available. For Private deployments you get customer-managed control plane options too.
[03:36] Sara Gomez: We are SOC2 and ISO17001 compliant — do you have a compliance matrix we can review? We also need data residency controls for EU workloads.
[03:44] Maya Patel: We'll include the compliance matrix. For data residency we support region pinning and private deployments targeted to EU regions.
[03:52] [00:00] Alex Kim: Let's move to the live simulation — Maya will kick off a burst test from three projects hitting the API simultaneously.
[04:00] Maya Patel: Kicking off now, you should see the Console's traffic chart and the per-project token burn. I'll simulate a 10x spike on project B.
[04:12] [noise] Maya Patel: You can see the allocator throttle lower-priority traffic and divert some requests to the quantized variant. There's a short 150-200ms penalty when we cold-start a new variant, but the overall per-token cost drops.
[04:30] Liam O'Neal: What about fairness — if a single org has multiple high-weight projects, do you support tenant-level caps to prevent noisy neighbor at the org level?
[04:38] Jordan Lee: Yes, you can set both org-level caps and project-level caps. The allocator respects both and will enforce the stricter of the two.
[04:45] Tom Wu: If we need guaranteed throughput for certain calls, is there an option for reserved capacity?
[04:50] Alex Kim: That's Redwood Dedicated — reserved GPU pools with committed throughput and SLA-backed latency targets. You can also combine Dedicated for critical workloads and Hosted for burst overflow via our smart routing.
[05:02] Priya Rao: Cost questions — how does billing work with mixed host/dedicated usage? We want predictable invoices.
[05:08] Alex Kim: Billing can be split by project keys; we'll show you a sample invoice mapping. For pilots we often do a monthly committed spend for Dedicated and metered usage for Hosted overflow. We'll put together a tailored pricing sheet.
[05:18] Sara Gomez: Any customers pushing large scale in EU with private deployments? We need references.
[05:23] Jordan Lee: We have a couple anonymized references in finance and health verticals; we'll share contactable references where allowed.
[05:30] [transcription error] Alex Kim: Oh — and on monitoring, the console has trace hooks so you can tie token-level costs to spans, though sometimes the agent names get munged in the UI — it's mostly fine.
[05:42] Liam O'Neal: On networking, if we go private VPC, does Redwood handle NAT/gateway or do we run the egress? Latency matters for us.
[05:50] Maya Patel: For Private deployments you manage your networking; we provide detailed architecture docs. For VPC peering we recommend colocated peering in the same region to minimize hop count. We'll include a network checklist.
[05:59] Tom Wu: About throttling behavior — do you provide client-side headers to indicate retry-after and lease tokens so our SDKs can implement backoff smoothly?
[06:07] Jordan Lee: Yes, the API returns structured headers including X-Redwood-Rate-Limit, X-Redwood-Lease and Retry-After. The SDKs honor them and support adaptive backoff. Occasionally the header names were different in early SDK versions — we'll call that out in the migration guide.
[06:21] Priya Rao: Great. Can we get a 2-week pilot with a controlled QPS cap so we can run our benchmark?
[06:27] Alex Kim: Absolutely, typically we spin up a POC org with project keys, configure quota slices, and run a benchmark suite with your models. We'll use the pilot to validate latency p99 and cost metrics.
[06:36] [crosstalk] Sarah Gomez: And security review?
[06:38] Maya Patel: We'll run a security review; I'll include our TEM for SOC2 controls and a network diagram.
[06:45] Alex Kim: Summarizing next steps: I'll send pilot pricing, Maya will share security and network docs by next Tuesday, and we'll schedule a kickoff with Liam and Tom for late April. Any other blockers?
[06:56] Priya Rao: Nothing major. We need to confirm token budget internally but otherwise good.
[07:00] Alex Kim: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links: pilot onboarding doc, sample policy YAML, and the security pack.
[07:07] Tom Wu: One more thing — can we instrument a test where client retries are disabled to see pure allocator behavior?
[07:12] Maya Patel: Yes we can run both with and without client-side retries; good point. We'll include that in the benchmark plan.
[07:18] Alex Kim: Alright, thanks all. We'll send the follow-ups.

End of meeting.
notes:
Demo included Console screen share of allocator, live burst test, and API header examples. Some words were mis-transcribed (kay-vee = KV), and occasional speaker attribution glitches. Customer asked for pilot, security docs, and benchmarks.
Shared links referenced during call: https://redwood.ai/docs/allocator, https://redwood.ai/security-pack, sample policy YAML in chat.
